newsitem.title: RWANDA: First Rwandans sentenced to death for genocide.
newsitem.headline: First Rwandans sentenced to death for genocide.

text.p: A Rwandan court sentenced two Rwandan Hutus to death on Friday for genocide and crimes against humanity, delivering the first death penalties for the 1994 slaughter of some 800,000 people.
State-run radio said Deogratias Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former administrator, had 15 days to appeal.

Both men received a four-hour trial on December 27 before a tribunal of three judges in the southeastern town of Kibungo where they were accused of organising massacres. They pleaded not guilty but had no defence lawyers.

They were the first suspects to go on trial under a genocide law passed last year. Some 90,000 Rwandans are crammed into jails accused of taking part in the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.

"They have been sentenced to death...and they have 15 days to appeal," Gerard Gahima, deputy justice minister, told Reuters in the capital Kigali, where separate genocide trials opened on December 30 and were adjourned.

Asked whether the two men received a fair trial without defence lawyers, Gahima said: "Under our law it is permissible for people to be tried without lawyers. If people think you can sweep the genocide of one million people under the carpet because there are no lawyers, they can think again."
"These crimes were committed in broad daylight. Either there were eyewitnesses or there were not. There are no complex legal issues involved. It is an issue of fact," Gahima added.
He said more trials were scheduled for next week but he had no details. Under Rwandan law, executions are by firing squad.
Observers in the Kibungo court on December 27 said the two defendants were booed and prosecutors were cheered from crowded public benches. Prosecutors passed written notes to the judges.
Human rights groups have welcomed the start of the trials but said they were superficial and flawed because of the lack of defence representation.

A Hutu Rwandan refugee lobby group, the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy to Rwanda, has dismissed the trials as "a mockery of justice" and said Hutu returnees being detained are being falsely accused by people who wanted their property.
The U.N. human rights office in Kigali said more than 2,000 Rwandan Hutus, part of 460,000 refugees who returned home from Tanzania last month, had been arrested as genocide suspects.
An international tribunal on the Rwandan genocide opened its first trials at its headquarters in Arusha, Tanzania, in 1996 but it cannot impose the death penalty on those found guilty.

Widely considered the worst mass slaughter in such a short period of time, the three-month genocide began on April 6, 1994, and ended when Tutsi rebels drove the Hutu-led government, its troops and militiamen into exile in Zaire and Tanzania.
"Some people feel public executions will serve as a lesson to those who might reconsider genocide but others are bound to cause an outcry about such executions," Gahima said.
"We don't subscribe to the belief there should be no justice because there are no lawyers," he added. "These trials are not something about which one feels good. But they must be done."
Some of the suspected masterminds of the 1994 killings are believed to be living in Africa, Europe and the United States.
